case_studies.title: The Table Says Otherwise: Testing LLMs with Counterfactual Relational Data
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer natural-language questions over structured data. However, when a table contains familiar real-world facts, it is unclear whether the model answers by reading the provided data or by recalling knowledge learned during pretraining. This distinction is important for database applications, where the provided tables should be the source of truth. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of determining whether large language models answer questions based on provided data or pre-existing knowledge. The authors built a benchmark called ContraTable to test this. The result helps evaluate the reliability of language models in database applications.

case_studies.title: INCARBench: A Benchmark for Scientific Configuration in VASP INCAR by Large Language Models
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into first-principles computational workflows, yet their ability to configure scientific calculations remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce INCARBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on input configuration for the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) through both configuration generation and repair tasks. Evaluating 19 model configurations reveals substantial capability differences among current frontier models. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of configuring scientific calculations in VASP by evaluating large language models on their ability to generate and repair input configurations. The researchers built a benchmark called INCARBench to test 19 model configurations. The result shows significant differences in capability among current models.

case_studies.title: MuPPET: A Benchmark for Contextual Privacy of LLM Assistants in Multi-Party Conversations
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in multi-party environments, handling sensitive personal data on behalf of individual users, for instance in group chats. When such an agent discloses private information, it reaches every group member at once. This risk is structurally harder to control than in one-to-one settings, as every piece of private information must be appropriate for every recipient in the group. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of privacy risks in group conversations with LLM agents, introducing a benchmark called MuPPET to measure these risks, and resulting in a tool to assess multi-party privacy exposure. The researchers built MuPPET to address the lack of existing benchmarks for multi-party settings. This research may have implications for IT teams managing LLM deployments in group chat environments.

case_studies.title: Can LLMs Reliably Self-Report Adversarial Prefills, and How?
case_studies.abstract: Prior work shows that large language models (LLMs) exhibit introspective capability on benign tasks. We extend the question to safety contexts and examine how reliably a model can recognize that its own prior response was elicited by an adversarial prefill attack. Across ten open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs (3B to 70B) and four safety benchmarks, no model reliably recognizes its own compromised outputs, with models claiming intent on prefilled responses at an average rate of $27.3\%$. case_studies.summary: This research looks at whether large language models can detect when they've been tricked into giving a wrong answer by an attacker. The study found that these models are not very good at recognizing when they've been compromised. The result is that models often claim they meant to give a bad answer, even when they didn't.

case_studies.title: On the Limits of Prompt-Conditioned Language Models as General-Purpose Learners
case_studies.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are frequently portrayed as general-purpose solvers capable of solving arbitrary tasks. We argue that this view overlooks a fundamental constraint: language is a compressed and capacity-limited interface for conveying task information. Modelling User--System interaction as a bilevel \emph{cheap-talk} game, we analyse how latent tasks are encoded into prompts and reinterpreted under alignment and safety constraints. case_studies.summary: This research challenges the idea that large language models can solve any task, finding that language has limitations in conveying task information. The authors built a model to analyse how tasks are encoded into prompts and reinterpreted under certain constraints. The result shows that language models have capacity limits and may not be as versatile as thought.

case_studies.title: Statistical Proof as a Window into Human-AI Collaboration: Practical Insights and a Community Agenda
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly woven into expert cognitive work in daily research, yet we know little about how human expertise should adapt when an AI system can execute substantial technical reasoning on its own. Here we use statistical proof development, a demanding and structured form of expert reasoning, as a window into this broader question. case_studies.summary: This research explores how human expertise can work with large language models, finding they can execute technical tasks with guidance but are unreliable without it. The study used statistical proof development to understand human-AI collaboration. The result shows LLMs have a limited but useful role in expert cognitive work.

case_studies.title: Litmus: Zero-Label, Code-Driven Metric Specification for Evaluating AI Systems
case_studies.abstract: As agentic LLM systems move from prototypes to deployment across increasingly diverse domains, evaluating them has become both more important and more difficult. The challenge is not only that individual metrics may be unreliable, but that evaluation goals are often left implicit. Without a clear account of what a system is expected to do, how it can fail, and which failures matter, metric choices become difficult to justify, interpret, or validate. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating AI systems by creating a zero-label system called Litmus, which designs evaluation and monitoring metrics for AI pipelines. Litmus helps to identify what a system is expected to do and how it can fail. The result is a more reliable and justified metric choice for AI system evaluation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI pipelines, here is what to do: review your current evaluation metrics, consider implementing Litmus to design new metrics, and validate your existing metrics against the new ones. This flags a risk: if your org uses unreliable metrics to evaluate AI systems, check your evaluation goals and metrics immediately. case_studies.abstract: This paper presents our algorithmic innovations for the NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge, focusing on Bit Manipulation Puzzles. In this task, the objective is to discover a hidden logical rule transforming input binary strings to outputs, then apply it to unseen inputs. The result is an improved ability for models to handle complex boolean logic and arithmetic without hallucinations.

case_studies.title: Causal Discovery in the Era of Agents
case_studies.abstract: Recent attempts to combine large language models (LLMs) with causal discovery ask models to infer pairwise directions, propose graph structures, or inject language-model outputs as priors and constraints. These approaches promise faster analysis, but they also obscure whether a causal evidence is supported by data and assumptions or by textual associations, prompt artifacts and hallucinated mechanisms. case_studies.title: SVD-Surgeon: Optimal Singular-Value Surgery for Large Language Model Compression
case_studies.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, but their deployment is constrained by substantial memory and compute requirements. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of large language models requiring substantial memory and compute resources by introducing SVD-Surgeon, a method that compresses these models without requiring retraining.
